title: 3-D shapes
summary: Recognise the {{term:cube-solid}}, {{term:cuboid}}, {{term:cylinder}}, {{term:cone}}, {{term:sphere}} and {{term:pyramid}}, count faces and edges, and make a net of a cube.
guide: 3-D shapes (like a box, a ball or a tin) take up space, unlike flat shapes. Children in England name them from Year 1 and count faces, edges and vertices in Year 2; Iran teaches them in grade 7 and Afghanistan in grade 6.

The first missions suit younger children too: they only tap the pictures. Read the sentences aloud if your child is not reading yet, and put real things next to the screen: a tin, a ball, a shoebox, a party hat.

A face is a flat surface of a solid, an edge is where two faces meet, and a {{term:vertex}} is a corner. In the pictures, edges at the back are drawn dashed. A common mistake is to count only the faces or edges you can see in the picture.
A net of a cube is six joined squares that fold up into a cube. Not every six squares make a net: six in a row, or two rows of three, do not fold into a cube.

find-cube.title: Find the cube
find-cube.prompt: Tap the {{term:cube-solid}}. A cube is like a dice: all its faces are the same size squares.
find-cube.hint: Look at the faces. Which shape looks the same from every side?
find-cube.success: Well done! That is a cube. It has 6 square faces, like a dice.
find-cube.why: What is the difference between a cube and a {{term:cuboid}}?
find-cube.model: Both have 6 faces and square corners. But all the faces of a cube are squares of the same size. A cuboid is longer, and some of its faces are rectangles, like a shoebox.

feedback.cuboid: The orange shape is long, like a shoebox. It is a {{term:cuboid}}. A cube's faces are all squares.
feedback.pyramid: The purple shape comes to a point. It is a {{term:pyramid}}.
feedback.extra: One of the shapes you tapped is not a cube. Tap it again to take it away.
feedback.missed: You have not tapped the cube yet.

can-roll.title: Which ones roll?
can-roll.prompt: Tap every shape that can roll.
can-roll.hint: A shape can roll if it has a curved surface. Three shapes do.
can-roll.success: Well done! The {{term:sphere}}, {{term:cylinder}} and {{term:cone}} have curved surfaces, so they roll.
can-roll.why: Why does a cylinder roll but a cube does not?
can-roll.model: A cube has only flat faces and sharp edges, so it stands on one face. A cylinder has a curved surface and rolls on it. If we stand it on one of its round flat faces, it stays still.

feedback.flat: That shape has only flat faces. It slides on a flat face but it does not roll. Tap it again to take it away.
feedback.extra: One of the shapes you tapped does not roll. Tap it again to take it away.
feedback.missed: There is one more shape that rolls. A cone rolls round in a circle.

cube-faces.title: How many faces?
cube-faces.prompt: A face is a flat surface of a solid. How many faces does a cube have? Tap the number.
cube-faces.hint: Turn a dice or a box in your hand. Count the top, bottom, front, back, left and right.
cube-faces.success: Well done! A cube has 6 faces, like a dice with 6 numbers.
cube-faces.why: Only 3 faces show in the picture. How do you know there are 6?
cube-faces.model: Each face we can see has an opposite face at the back: top and bottom, front and back, left and right. 3 faces show and 3 are hidden, so 3 + 3 = 6

feedback.seen-only: 3 faces show in the picture, but there are faces at the back too. Think of a dice.
feedback.sides-only: There are 4 faces round the sides. Count the top and the bottom too.
feedback.too-big: Too many. Picture a dice: top, bottom, front, back, left and right.
feedback.too-small: Too few. Count the faces at the back and underneath too.

pyramid-edges.title: Edges of a pyramid
pyramid-edges.prompt: An edge is where two faces meet. This {{term:pyramid}} has a square base. How many edges does it have? The dashed lines are edges at the back.
pyramid-edges.hint: Count the edges round the base first, then the edges that go up to the top.
pyramid-edges.success: Well done! 4 edges round the base and 4 up to the top: 4 + 4 = 8
pyramid-edges.why: How many edges does a pyramid with a triangle for its base have? How do you know?
pyramid-edges.model: The triangle base has 3 edges, and one edge goes up from each corner of the base to the top: 3 more. So 3 + 3 = 6 edges. Every pyramid has twice as many edges as its base has sides.

feedback.solid-lines: You counted only the solid lines. The dashed lines are edges at the back, and they count too.
feedback.base-only: The base has 4 edges. Count the edges that go up from the base to the top too.
feedback.too-big: Too many. Check you counted each edge only once.
feedback.too-small: Too few. Count the dashed edges at the back and the edges up to the top.

cube-net.title: A net of a cube
cube-net.prompt: Shade six squares that would fold up into a closed {{term:cube-solid}} if you cut them out and folded along the lines.
cube-net.hint: One way: four squares in a row (round the sides of the cube) and one above and one below that row (the top and the bottom).
cube-net.success: Well done! That is a net of a cube: when it is folded, each square becomes one face.
cube-net.why: Why don't six squares in a row make a cube?
cube-net.model: If we fold six squares in a row, four of them wrap round the sides and the fifth and sixth land on faces that are already covered. Then the top and bottom are left open. In a net, each square must cover a different face.

feedback.empty: Tap the squares to shade them.
feedback.too-few: A cube has 6 faces, so you need 6 squares.
feedback.too-many: A cube has only 6 faces. Take a square away.
feedback.not-net: If you fold this, two squares land on the same face and one face is left open. Move the squares; try a cross shape.
